passage: When the result list went up on the notice board, Keerthana found her name at the top and felt her chest swell. She'd won the state-level design prize. Her friends pressed around her. Sahil, who had spent three weekends helping her fix her prototype, stood at the back. Keerthana pushed through the crowd and hugged him. "Half of this is you." She then told the others she had been wrong about the dimensions until he caught it, and she thanked her professor by name. When another student said, "I bet the rest didn't even try," Keerthana shook her head. "They worked hard too. I was lucky with the judges." That evening she texted her mother, and only then let herself squeal.

qa.q: How many weekends did Sahil spend helping Keerthana?
qa.a: He spent three weekends helping her.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when she found her name, and how did she show humility?
qa.a: She felt proud, and she showed humility by crediting Sahil and her professor and by saying the others worked hard too.

qa.q: What could Keerthana do to keep the win from creating distance?
qa.a: She could keep thanking helpers, celebrate with the group and listen to those who did not win.

qa.q: How might Sahil feel about being credited?
qa.a: Sahil probably feels appreciated and included, which strengthens the friendship.

grounding: Keerthana celebrates a prize by crediting Sahil and her professor and not putting others down.

passage:
"You got it?" Farhan asked, dropping his bag by the door.
"The internship. Yes." Ganga couldn't stop smiling.
"That's huge. Tell me everything."
"It's mostly luck, honestly. And you helped me practise the case question four times."
"Five. But who's counting."
She laughed. "I don't want to be that person who goes on about it. My cousin also applied and didn't get it."
"So don't post the news all over. Tell your family, tell the people who helped, and be kind about your cousin."
"I called Grandma first. She cried."
"Then you did it right." Farhan grinned. "Dinner is on you, though."
"Deal. Somewhere cheap."

qa.q: Who did Ganga call first?
qa.a: She called Grandma first.

qa.q: What is Ganga worried about even though she is happy?
qa.a: She worries about being someone who goes on about her success and about her cousin who did not get the job, so she is trying to celebrate without hurting anyone.

qa.q: What could Ganga do to share the news kindly?
qa.a: She could tell family and helpers, thank Farhan, and be gentle with her cousin instead of announcing it widely.

qa.q: How might Ganga's cousin feel about the news?
qa.a: The cousin may feel disappointed and a little envious, and would probably want to hear it in a gentle, private way.

grounding: Ganga shares her success, credits Farhan and tempers her pride out of care for her cousin.

passage: The day I won the inter-college debate in Guwahati, I wanted to shout it from the rooftop. I'm Binita. The trophy was heavy and shiny, and people kept clapping me on the back. At the celebration dinner, one of the boys from the other team said, a bit sourly, "Well, you got the easy side of the motion." A sharp reply rose in my throat: something about how they couldn't have won with any side. I swallowed it. Instead I said, "Your rebuttal on point three nearly finished me." He smiled, surprised. Then I thought of Salma, my teammate, who'd stayed up two nights researching the statistics I'd quoted, and who'd been too shy to speak on stage. When I gave my short thank-you, I said her name first. She went red and hid her face in her hands. We still keep that trophy on her shelf, not mine.

qa.q: Where does the trophy stay now?
qa.a: On Salma's shelf.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling when the boy from the other team made the sour remark?
qa.a: Binita felt a flash of irritation and pride, with a sharp reply rising, but chose to hold it back.

qa.q: What did Binita do that showed pride with humility?
qa.a: Binita praised the opponent's rebuttal instead of boasting and thanked Salma first for the research behind the win.

qa.q: How did Salma react to being thanked first?
qa.a: She went red and hid her face, suggesting she felt shy but touched to be recognised.

grounding: Shows a young adult celebrating a win by acknowledging help and avoiding putting others down.

passage:
Coach's note, university athletics meet, Saturday.
Rashmi won the women's 800 metres today, her first gold. She crossed the line, dropped to her knees, then got up and went straight to hug Irawati, who had paced her for the first 400 in every training session this term. On the podium she waved to the whole team stand, not just her family. When the local reporter asked her secret, she said, "My coach's plan and Irawati's pacing. And a lot of early mornings." I've seen other winners this season make a show of it, dancing in front of the runners who lost, and I watched how quickly the team mood soured around them. Rashmi's way does the opposite. The girls who didn't medal crowded round her afterwards, laughing. Irawati looked quietly proud all afternoon. I'll mention this at Monday's team meeting as the example to follow.
— Coach Menon

qa.q: What race did Rashmi win?
qa.a: The women's 800 metres.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling after Rashmi's win?
qa.a: She looked quietly proud all afternoon, glad to have her pacing recognised.

qa.q: What did Rashmi do that strengthened the team?
qa.a: She thanked Irawati and the coach, waved to the whole team, and credited early mornings instead of boasting.

qa.q: How did the team react to Rashmi's way of celebrating?
qa.a: The girls who didn't medal crowded round her laughing, unlike the soured mood around winners who showed off.

grounding: Shows a young adult celebrating success by acknowledging help and effort, which builds shared pride rather than distance.

passage:
Thursday.
Got the state scholarship! Full fees and hostel. I read the email five times.
My first instinct was to post it everywhere, all caps. I actually typed, "TOLD YOU ALL I'D DO IT." Then I thought about Rafi and Joel, who applied too and didn't get it. And about how that post would feel to them. Deleted it.
Instead I called Ammi first. She cried. Then I texted Madhuri, who spent three evenings helping me fix my essay: "We did it. Your edits are in there." She replied with twenty exclamation marks.
In the evening I posted just a photo of my acceptance letter with "Grateful to everyone who helped. Especially Madhuri and Ammi." Rafi commented "Congrats bro, well deserved." That felt better than any all-caps post could have.
— Wasim

qa.q: Who spent three evenings helping Wasim fix the essay?
qa.a: Madhuri.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling when first reading the email?
qa.a: Wasim felt thrilled and proud, reading it five times and wanting to post it everywhere.

qa.q: What made Wasim's final post better than the first draft?
qa.a: It thanked the people who helped instead of boasting, which was kinder to friends who didn't get the scholarship.

qa.q: How did Rafi respond to the post?
qa.a: He commented "Congrats bro, well deserved," showing the humble post let him feel happy for Wasim.

grounding: Shows a young adult celebrating a scholarship by acknowledging help and avoiding boasting that could hurt others.
